Business plan text:

Steadyhand Grips
STEADYHAND GRIPS
Executive Summary
Problem
Millions of Americans live with arthritis, essential tremor, Parkinsons and other conditions
that effect there hands. For these people everyday tasks like stirring a pot, using a peeler or
pruning roses becomes painful and sometimes impossible. This loss of ability is not just a
physical problem it is a emotional one as well, because cooking and gardening are things that
give people a sense of purpose and independance. When they can no longer do them they often
have to rely on family members or caregivers which impacts quality of life in a big way. We
believe this is a significant problem that is not being addressed properly in todays market.
Solution
Steadyhand Grips is a custom solution that addresses this problem head on. We take a mold of
each customers hand using a safe moldable material, and then we create a grip made to fit that
exact hand which attaches to the persons existing utensils and tools. Because every hand is
different, and every condition is different, our approach is personal and tailored rather than
one size fits all. The grip is made from durable materials that is comfortable and easy to
clean. Along with the grip we provide a fitting service, where one of our team members works
with the customer to make sure the grip is right and adjust it if needed. This combination of a
physical product and a personal service is what makes Steadyhand unique and gives customers a
feeling of being cared for.
Market
The market for our product is very large. According to our research there are tens of millions
of adults in the United States with some form of arthritis and many more with other hand
conditions, and this number is growing every year as the population gets older. Baby boomers
are retiring and want to stay active and independant for as long as possible. If even a small
percentage of these people were to purchase our grips this would be a multi million dollar
opportunity. We also believe there is potential in related markets such as occupational
therapy, assisted living facilities, and eventually the general consumer market for ergonomic
tools. The adaptive products space is expanding rapidly and we are positioned to take advantage
of this trend.
Business Model
Our business model is based on selling custom grips along with the fitting service. Customers
would pay for the fitting and the grip together, and we may also offer additional grips for
other tools at a lower price. We are still determining our exact pricing but we are looking at
somewhere between a fair price that customers can afford and a price that allows us to be
profitable. In the future we may also explore subscription options, partnerships with
therapists and clinics, and selling through retail channels. We think there are many different
ways to generate revenue and we will figure out which is best as we grow and learn more about
our customers needs. Our costs will include materials, molding supplies, labor for the
fittings, and marketing.
Competition
There are existing companies that sell adaptive kitchen tools and ergonomic grips, and some of
them have been around for a long time. However we believe that our product is different because
it is truly custom and comes with a personal service. Most of the competition sells standard
sized foam handles or thick utensils that dont fit everyone. Some people also make there own
grips at home using tape or putty. We believe our customers will pay more for something that is
made for them specifically. We also think that our team is more passionate and more agile then
larger companies who may be slow to respond to customer feedback. Our personal approach is

something that is difficult for others to copy, although we know that competitors could try.
Team
Brianna Kowalczyk is our CEO and a junior studying business, she came up with the idea after
watching her grandmother struggle in the kitchen because of arthritis. She leads strategy,
sales and customer relationships. Dev Raghunathan is our CTO and is a senior studying
mechanical engineering, he designed our prototype and handles the molding process and
materials. Tyler Okonkwo-Banks is our head of operations and is a sophomore studying marketing,
he manages our fittings, our social media and our website. Together we bring a mix of business,
technical and creative skills and we are all very passionate about helping people. We have also
spoken with a few advisors including a professor and a local occupational therapist who have
given us helpful feedback, although they are not formally part of the company.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have achieved several important milestones. We have formed a C Corp, built a working
prototype of our grip, launched a website, and most importantly we have our first paying
client, who purchased a set of grips for her kitchen and gardening tools and said she was very
happy with them. This proves that people are willing to pay for what we are offering. We have
spent a small amount of our own money on materials and legal fees. Our financial projections
show strong growth over the next three years, with revenue growing quickly as we reach more
customers, and we expect to become profitable once we reach enough scale. We are confident that
the numbers will work out because the demand is so large and our product provides so much value
to customers.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to this competition for funding that will help us take Steadyhand Grips to the
next level. With the prize money we would purchase better molding equipment, hire part time
help for the fittings, improve our website, and do more marketing to reach new customers. We
are also looking for mentorship from experienced entrepreneurs and connections to potential
partners such as clinics and senior living communities. Beyond the money, being part of this
competition would give us credibility and visibility which are very important for a young
company like ours. We believe that Steadyhand has the potential to change the lives of many
people and we would be honored to have the chance to share our vision with the judges. Thank
you for considering our application and we look forward to the opportunity to grow with your
support.

Question: What can the team do to improve their written submission?

response.text:
The team can improve their written submission by:

1. **Clarifying the problem statement**: The problem is described but lacks specific data or emotional impact. Including statistics on the number of affected individuals, the cost of caregiving, or the psychological effects of losing independence would strengthen the problem statement.

2. **Quantifying the market opportunity**: While the market is described as large, specific numbers (e.g., estimated market size, growth rate, or target customer segments) would add credibility and clarity.

3. **Defining the value proposition more clearly**: The solution is described, but the unique value proposition (e.g., customization, personal service, durability) should be more explicitly tied to customer needs and competitive advantages.

4. **Structuring the business model more formally**: The business model is outlined but lacks a clear revenue model, cost structure, and customer segments. Using a lean startup or business model canvas format would improve clarity.

5. **Enhancing the competitive analysis**: The competition section is brief and lacks a SWOT analysis or differentiation matrix. Highlighting specific advantages (e.g., personal service, customization, agility) and addressing potential threats would strengthen this section.

6. **Improving the team section**: The team section is brief and lacks detail on individual roles, relevant experience, and how the team’s skills complement each other. Including specific achievements or past projects would add credibility.

7. **Adding financial details**: The financials section is vague. Including projected revenue, profit margins, break-even point, and key assumptions would provide a clearer picture of the business’s financial viability.

8. **Enhancing the milestones section**: The milestones are listed but lack context or metrics. Including specific KPIs (e.g., number of customers, revenue targets, customer satisfaction rates) would make the progress more measurable.

9. **Improving the ask section**: The ask is described but lacks specificity. Including a detailed breakdown of how the funds will be used, projected outcomes, and a timeline for achieving key goals would make the ask more compelling.

10. **Proofreading and editing**: The submission contains grammatical errors and formatting issues that detract from professionalism. A thorough review and editing process would improve readability and credibility.
